prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B024, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full first-round exchange the scientific case looks stronger to me, because the objections raised against it concern boundary and wording, not the result. The result is a specific invention (the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the differential light shift while holding many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts), followed by a realization that took systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18, reproduced in several laboratories and species and confirmed in intercontinental comparisons. That is a different regime from the frequency comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012): those supply the optical-to-microwave link and the quantum control of one particle, while the lattice clock gains its stability by interrogating a large ensemble without perturbing the transition. I think the citation should say this explicitly, as several colleagues asked, and I have rewritten my citation accordingly. The concrete consequences are tests of constant drift and of new physics, relativistic geodesy and the route to a redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is compact: Katori for the concept and first realization, Ye for taking the platform to record accuracy and for the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock regime, which I regard as physics and not only engineering.
statement.case_against: The reservations I hold are real and I have not dissolved them. First, a third prize in a lineage that already includes the comb and ion-trap control invites the reading that this is refinement of honoured ground, and Danielsson's point that a new state of matter carries more discovery content than a better measurement is a legitimate criterion that I cannot rule out by argument alone. Second, the two-name limit leaves out Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, and I cannot settle from the supplied record whether any of them has a claim that displaces Ye. Third, the redefinition of the second is still pending, so the practical payoff is prospective. I weigh the third as weak because the physics is already established. The first is the one I take most seriously, and it is a difference of judgment about what the prize is for, not a defect in the evidence.

responses.point: Danielsson calls B024 a refined invention that sharpens a measurement we already knew how to make, whereas twisted bilayer graphene revealed an unexpected state of matter, and says four first places show where measurement specialists cluster; he would not oppose B024 if discussion converges there.
responses.response: I accept the point that the opening count is not an argument, and I do not use it as one. On kind, I would say that the lattice clock is not only a better version of a known measurement: reaching 1e-18 required a new regime, many atoms interrogated at a magic wavelength with Fermi-degenerate many-body effects that had to be understood and controlled, and the ensemble physics is part of the result. I also grant that B003 has the stronger new-phase-of-matter character. Where I still differ is on readiness for a clean award. The pairing mechanism is open, and the three-name limit excludes the first experimental author, whom you name as Yuan Cao, and the early confirming groups. If the committee judges that interpretive maturity is not required, as the high-temperature superconductor precedent you cite suggests, then B003 becomes a serious competitor and I would need the credit question settled first. I have therefore kept it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson regards B024 as the best-attributed and most mature candidate but weights the new-phase-of-matter character of the moire discovery above an improvement in precision, however spectacular, and agrees that a second circuit prize so soon after 2025 is hard to justify.
responses.response: I appreciate that you say plainly that B024 is the better-attributed and more mature case, because the disagreement then comes down to one weighting. I would argue that a precision result is a discovery when it opens measurements that were impossible before, as 1e-18 clocks do for gravitational redshift over centimetres and for constant-drift limits, and not only when it reveals a new phase. I also take your own caution about Bistritzer versus earlier twist-angle band-structure work seriously, since it bears on whether the theory credit in B003 can be drawn cleanly. On B043, thank you; I confirm that I am not advocating it and I do not need the committee to discuss it.

responses.point: Mehlig could support B024 as his first alternative if the citation says precisely what is new, namely Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of many atoms at a magic wavelength, and not just a better clock, given the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-clock prize.
responses.response: I agree and I have drafted the citation to do exactly that: it names the magic-wavelength confinement and the removal of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors, and it states the 1e-18 outcome. That wording separates the lattice clock from the comb, which supplies the frequency link, and from single-ion control, where a single particle limits the signal-to-noise. I also note your own frank assessment that B006 has the weakest support on the table and weaker quantitative confirmation of the exponents. I do not hold that against the physics, but it is why I cannot support B006 as a final configuration.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's contribution is best credited as co-invention or as realization to record accuracy, and says the citation wording depends on it; she also would not treat the comb and ion-clock prizes as making this a pure successor.
responses.response: On the question you pose, I would credit Ye for realization and for the many-body regime, not for co-invention of the magic-wavelength idea, which I attribute to Katori. The citation I propose reflects that, since it says 'invention and realization' and describes the confinement scheme in the abstract, without assigning authorship of the idea to either name alone. I accept that this leaves open the chronology you say you cannot check, and if the committee established that another group's proposal or first demonstration preceded or paralleled Katori's, I would reopen the pair. I also appreciate that you do not discount my merit view of other areas because of my Chalmers ties; that is a kind judgment but I will keep my own disclosure strict.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, notes that a metrology prize risks being read as an instrument achievement and not a discovery, that the SI second has not yet been redefined, and that B003 and B023 have a stronger claim to opening a field.
responses.response: I think the redefinition should not be a prerequisite: the Nobel criterion is the discovery or invention and its demonstrated consequences, and those are already in hand, whereas the redefinition is a metrological decision that depends on the committee on units and on consensus among national laboratories, so waiting would tie our timing to a process outside physics discovery. On instrument versus discovery, I would say that the magic-wavelength lattice is a physical idea, a way to engineer the atomic Stark shift to zero, before it is an instrument. I accept the force of your concern about B023 after the 2016 prize, and I am not carrying it as my alternative for that reason.

responses.point: Kroll discloses a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory and asks whether the committee needs to consider recusal on the clock discussion, while also arguing that the citation must state why lattice clocks are distinct from comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I think a doctoral research stay in a laboratory whose comb work is a background to B024, with no tie to Katori or Ye, is a disclosure and not a reason for recusal, and I would be content to leave the ruling to the chair. It does mean that your argument for distinction carries more weight when it is explicit, so I support your suggestion to put the distinction in the citation. I also noted that you and I read the record the same way, so my agreement with you adds no independent evidence and I will not count it as such.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg, Ludlow, Hinkley or the ion-clock leaders have a claim that should change the credited pair, which the supplied record does not settle.
Whether the committee accepts the distinction from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as stated in the citation, or still reads B024 as a third prize in one lineage.
Whether metrology counts as discovery for this prize, and how much weight to give the new-phase-of-matter character of B003 against clean credit and maturity in B024.
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism and the omitted first experimental author in B003 will be resolved enough to make it the better choice.
I rely on my recollection of the literature, not on a verified chronology of the lattice-clock proposals.
statement.conflict_note: I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT. My profile records Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum, and Chalmers hosted researchers tied to the 2025 prize. This remains a specific recusal issue for B043 (circuit quantum electrodynamics), which I do not advocate and would not vote for. No specific conflict is apparent for B024, B003 or B014. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye. I note the disclosures by Kroll and Olsson on B024 and consider them matters for the chair; I see nothing in them that changes my reading of the science.
